text: Every action you take in Azure happens inside a subscription, and understanding what a subscription actually is, is the real starting point for managing Azure at any scale. It's not just a login you were handed on day one - it's a billing boundary and a scope for permissions, and both of those have real consequences for how an organization structures its cloud footprint.

Run az account show and you'll see the subscription you're currently working in, including its ID and the Microsoft Entra tenant it belongs to. az account list shows every subscription your account can access, which matters once you're juggling more than one. az account set switches which subscription your CLI commands target - get this wrong in a script and you could deploy production resources into a test subscription, or the other way around, without any error warning you it happened.

A subscription does two jobs at once. First, it's a billing boundary - every resource inside it rolls up into one invoice, which is why companies commonly split subscriptions by department, project, or environment rather than running everything through a single one. Second, it's a scope - role assignments and Azure Policy applied at the subscription level apply to everything deployed inside it automatically, with no extra configuration required resource by resource.

Once an organization has more than a handful of subscriptions, repeating the same RBAC assignment or policy on each one stops scaling, and it's easy to accidentally miss one. az account management-group create sets up a management group, and az account management-group subscription add moves an existing subscription under it - now one role assignment or policy at the management group level covers every subscription nested inside it, automatically.

Azure's hierarchy nests five levels: the Microsoft Entra tenant at the top, management groups below it - nestable up to six levels deep - then subscriptions, then resource groups, then the individual resources themselves. Permissions and policy both flow downward through this entire chain, which is exactly why getting the grouping right at the top saves a huge amount of repetitive work everywhere below it.

That hierarchy is also where every resource eventually lives - inside a resource group, one level below the subscription. Next up: resource groups themselves, and Azure Resource Manager, the single layer every Azure action actually goes through, no matter which tool you used to send it.
